text: You've been learning your whole life,
but you've probably been doing it half
as well as you could. But that can
change today. Whether you want to
quickly sound knowledgeable on a subject
at work, ace a certification exam, or
level up your pickle ball game to beat
your friends, you can do it surprisingly
quick by focusing on five metalarning
skills backed by science. State
optimization, mistake optimization,
active recall, reduction, and turning
off. They form the acronym S M A R T. I
figured if goal setting had a smart
acronym, learning needed one, too. So
the next time you need to learn
something new, use the SM A T framework
to cut your learning time in half.
Metalarning skill number one, state
optimization.
In Peak, the definitive book on learning
and mastering well-defined skills,
Anders Ericson uses the word intense 18
times to describe how high performers
practice. Every worldass performer he
observed, from chess champions analyzing
complex endgame positions to violinists
rehearsing tricky passages, entered a
state of intense concentration to
maximize learning. To master any
material fast, you must ratchet up your
ability to intensely focus before your
learning sessions.
Most people just eliminate distractions.
They go to a quiet room, put on
noiseancelling headphones, and silence
their phone. Better learners go a step
further and clear mental clutter. As Cal
Newport explains, in deep work, they
eliminate attention residue by writing
down anything lingering in their head,
worries, obligations, unfinished
thoughts, and park them to think about
later. But the best learners do
something surprising. They do 15 to 30
minutes of moderately intense exercise
before learning. Whether it's running,
biking, or playing a sport, they elevate
their heart rate enough to break a sweat
but not exhaust themselves.
Why? Elevating your heart rate increases
blood flow to the brain, delivering more
oxygen and glucose to fuel an intense
study session. Along with increased
blood flow comes a neurochemical flood
of dopamine and noradrenaline that
enhances focus. Add in the production of
BDNF, a protein that helps form new
connections in the brain, and you're in
the optimal learning state. The book
Spark dedicates multiple chapters to
this phenomenon. One study found that
students who elevated their heart rate
by running before class saw significant
increases in reading comprehension and
grades compared to their peers.
Metalarning skill number two, mistake
optimization.
Making the most of your learning time
means making more mistakes, just not too
many. Mistakes are one of the brain's
best learning hacks. Every time you slip
up, your anterior singulate cortex
sounds an internal alarm, which lights
up your memory circuits, making whatever
you focus on next more likely to stick.
But there's a limit. Too many mistakes
flood the system with stress and shut
down learning. Luckily, learning science
has revealed a sweet spot. 8515.
Succeed about 85% of the time and fail
A 15% failure rate keeps your brain
challenged, alert, and primed for growth
without tipping into this sucks, I want
to quit mode. Leverage the 8515 rule by
designing practice drills with an 85%
success rate. If you're learning to play
the guitar, adjust the difficulty of
your chord transitions so you're
screwing up just three times for every
20 attempts. If you're learning to serve
a tennis ball, adjust the target zone
until you can land 17 out of 20 serves.
When learning a new subject, tell an AI
chatbot, "Give me 10 sentence completion
exercises using the following material.
If I get more than eight right, make the
next set harder. If I get fewer than
eight, make it easier." But remember
this above all else. When you make a
mistake, resist looking at the answer
and moving on. Instead, let the sting
linger as you understand why you got it
wrong. That's how real growth happens.
Metalarning skill number three, active
recall.
Make it stick is my favorite book on
studying and it boils down to one
message. Effort equals retention.
The more you work to retrieve
information without looking at notes,
the more likely you'll retain that
information. Struggling to recall
information creates strong and smooth
neural pathways. Think of it like paving
a trail through a forest. Each time you
struggle to find your way, you clear the
brush and pack the dirt a little firmer.
The next time you're having a
conversation and need to recall
information you've just learned, you can
race down that path and access it with
ease.
Simply reviewing your notes doesn't give
you the same easy recall abilities.
Therefore, if you want what you learn to
stick, build these three active recall
habits. Habit number one, periodic
pause. After 5 to 10 minutes of
learning, pause and repeat what you've
just learned out loud. For example, when
you listen to an audio book, pause every
10 minutes and pair it back the most
important points and stories as though
you're explaining them to a friend.
Habit number two, end of session recap.
At the end of a learning session,
explain everything you just learned
aloud as if you're teaching someone.
Then, write down three to five keywords
that capture the main ideas you want to
remember. Add them at the top of your
notes or in a dedicated recall list so
you can easily find them next time.
Habit number three, start of session
recall. Before diving into new material,
spend 2 minutes explaining what the
keywords from your last learning session
mean without looking at your notes.
Remember, if you find retrieving
information from memory difficult,
that's a good thing. Effort to retrieve
equals retention.
Metalarning skill number four,
reduction.
Reduce what you're learning to one
thing. One acronym, one sentence, one
page, or one visual. One acronym.
Turning what I learned about learning
into a smart acronym took effort, but
it's something I'll remember for the
rest of my life. One sentence. After
reading Atomic Habits, I tried to
capture the essence of what I learned in
a single sentence. Small improvements
compound over time, so focus on building
systems rather than chasing goals.
The effort to refine that sentence makes
me more likely to remember it. One page.
When I studied negotiation for a month,
I reduced everything I learned to a
single page cheat sheet with six key
tactics.
One visual. When learning about space
repetition, I understood the concept
better after I took out a sheet of paper
and drew a series of forgetting curves
that got progressively flatter after
active recall. The more you can compress
and simplify what you learn, the greater
you'll understand and retain it.
Complexity fades from memory. Simplicity
endures.
Metalarning skill number five, turning
off. The last but most important skill
to accelerate learning is to turn off
your conscious mind and let your brain
consolidate what you learned as you
rest. You can think of studying and
practicing as drafting the blueprints
for improvement. When you sleep, your
brain uses those blueprints to renovate
itself.
Sleep is often an afterthought when
people strive to master a subject. But
in Peak, Anders Ericson's research shows
that masters prioritize sleep, averaging
about 1.5 hours more each night than the
typical adult. Matthew Walker's research
in why we sleep found it's not just
nighttime sleep that enhances learning.
It's also daytime naps. The difference
between a group who napped during the
day and another who didn't was a 20%
greater ability to recall information at
6 p.m. that day.
Sleep in the form of a full night's rest
or a midday nap not only cements what
you just learned, it also refreshes the
hippocampus so you can learn and retain
more information in your next learning
session.
So if you want to sound smart and look
skilled in record time, focus on the
smart learning framework every study
session or practice. State optimization.
Elevate your heart rate for 15 to 30
minutes before your learning session to
flood your brain with focusenhancing
neurochemicals. Mistake optimization.
Design practice drills to hit the 8515
sweet spot. Active recall. Periodically
retrieve recent lessons from memory
without looking at notes. Reduction.
Always try to simplify and condense what
you learn into an acronym, a sentence, a
page, or a visual to make it stick. And
then turn off. Make sleep a priority
because that's when your brain
consolidates and cements what you've
learned.
